title: Tunnel Diodes, RTDs and Tunnel Transistors

questions.q: A tunnel diode is a p–n junction doped about a thousand times more heavily than usual. What does the heavy doping do?
options: It makes the depletion region (the wall) very thin, only about 10 nm
It makes the depletion region much wider, about 1 µm
It removes the band gap, so the junction becomes a metal
It makes the junction give out light when current flows
questions.explain: Very heavy doping (10¹⁹–10²⁰ cm⁻³) makes the depletion region, the wall, only about 10 nm thick, thin enough to tunnel through. It also moves the Fermi level into the bands, giving filled states on the n side that can face empty states on the p side.

questions.q: What rule decides whether an electron can tunnel across a tunnel diode's junction?
options: It keeps its energy, so it needs an empty state at the same energy on the other side
It must gain extra energy from the voltage before it can tunnel
It can tunnel only if the other side has no electrons at all
It can tunnel only when the junction is reverse-biased
questions.explain: Tunnelling keeps the electron's energy, so it can only tunnel into an empty state at the same energy opposite. The current flows when filled states face empty ones.

questions.q: The graph shows a tunnel diode's current (solid) and the three parts that add up to it (dashed and dotted). Which part makes the first hump, the peak?
questions.alt: Current against voltage: a solid total curve with a peak near 0.07 V and a valley near 0.33 V; dashed and dotted curves labelled tunnelling, ordinary diode and excess (defects)
options: The tunnelling current
The ordinary diode current
The excess current through defects
None of them: the peak comes from heat
questions.explain: Tunnelling makes the first hump, the ordinary diode current makes the final rise, and a small excess current through defect states fills the valley. The peak-to-valley current ratio (about 5.6 here) is the tunnel diode's figure of merit.

questions.q: The graph shows a tunnel diode's current against voltage. What happens in the shaded region, between the peak and the valley?
questions.alt: Current against voltage: the current rises to a peak near 0.07 V, falls through a shaded region to a valley near 0.33 V, then rises steeply
options: More voltage gives less current: negative differential resistance
More voltage gives more current, as in an ordinary resistor
The current stays the same whatever the voltage
No current flows at all
questions.explain: Between the peak and the valley, more voltage gives less current: the change in voltage divided by the change in current is negative, so this is called negative differential resistance. (The diode still absorbs power, because current and voltage themselves are both positive.)

questions.q: What is a tunnel diode's falling region (negative differential resistance) most useful for?
options: Making oscillators: it cancels a resonant circuit's losses, so the oscillation keeps going
Making solar cells: it turns light into current
Making lasers: it gives out light at the valley
Making fuses: it cuts the current when it gets too large
questions.explain: A resonant circuit rings and dies away because of its losses. Biased in its falling (negative-resistance) region, a tunnel diode cancels those losses, so the oscillation grows and then keeps going.

questions.q: A resonant-tunnelling diode has two thin walls with a quantum well between them. Why does an electron at one particular energy pass through both walls almost every time?
options: Its energy matches the level in the well (resonance)
It has enough energy to go over both walls
At that energy the two walls become thinner
At that energy the electron loses its charge
questions.explain: When the electron's energy matches the level in the well (resonance), the waves reflected from the two walls cancel, and it passes almost every time. At other energies it is almost always reflected: a sharp energy filter.

questions.q: What are resonant-tunnelling diodes best known for?
options: The fastest electronic oscillators at room temperature, reaching nearly 2 THz
The most efficient solar cells ever made, above 50% efficiency
The brightest blue LEDs, used in all white lighting
The largest memory chips, storing terabytes on one die
questions.explain: RTDs are the fastest electronic oscillators at room temperature: 650 GHz in 1997, 1.98 THz in 2017. Their weakness is tiny output power, typically microwatts at the highest frequencies.

questions.q: Why can an ordinary MOSFET not switch more steeply than about 60 mV per tenfold change in current at room temperature?
options: When it is off, only the few 'hot' electrons with enough energy get over the barrier, and their number falls only so fast
Its source and drain contacts have too much resistance for a faster switch
Its channel is too long for the electrons to reach the drain quickly
Its electrons tunnel through the gate oxide and cancel part of the gate voltage
questions.explain: A MOSFET lets electrons over a barrier set by the gate. When it is meant to be off, only the hot tail of electrons gets over, and that tail sets the 60 mV per decade limit: it is set by temperature, not by the oxide or the contacts. So supply voltages have hardly fallen in twenty years.

questions.q: The picture compares a MOSFET with a tunnel FET. How does the tunnel FET try to switch more steeply than 60 mV per decade?
questions.alt: Left: energy bands of a MOSFET with an n-type source. Middle: energy bands of a tunnel FET with a p+ source. Right: illustrative switching curves for the two
options: Electrons tunnel through the barrier from the source instead of going over it, which cuts off the hot tail
Its gate oxide is thinner, so the gate pulls the channel's bands down harder
Its channel is shorter, so electrons cross before they have time to scatter
Its source is more heavily doped, so more hot electrons get over the barrier
questions.explain: In a tunnel FET the source is p-type. The gate pulls the channel's band below the source's filled valence band, opening a window. Electrons above the top of the valence band have nothing to tunnel into, so the hot tail is cut off and switching can be steeper.

questions.q: True or false: tunnel FETs are already used in mainstream computer chips.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Laboratory tunnel FETs beat 60 mV per decade, usually only at very low currents, but tunnelling passes far fewer electrons than going over a barrier, so circuits would be slow. They remain research in 2026.
